CONGRANT.TITLE: NSF Center for Equity in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich (CEE-E3)
Broadening Participation in STEM
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is located in the historic Texan borderlands created at the end of the Mexican-American war in 1848 which separated families on both sides of the Rio Grande River. The university was formed in 2013 when The University of Texas at Brownsville and The University of Texas Pan-American were consolidated to expand educational opportunities in the underserved and rural Valley of the Rio Grande. UTRGV is a major Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI), primarily a nonresidential, 4-year, public, R2 institution, with campuses situated along the lower 100 miles of the Rio Grande. UTRGV's student demographics mirror those of the Lower Rio Grande Valley (RGV), with over 95% of our 32,000 students being of Hispanic or Latinx origin (Region One Education Service Center, 2021), and over 85% having Mexican-American heritage. Academic programs in engineering, started in 1992, were first accredited by ABET in 1996. The College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) currently has 6 departments offering 8 bachelors' and 7 masters' degrees. The college has over 110 faculty members and serves nearly 3900 students, mostly (90%) undergraduates. Although CECS does not have a PhD program yet, a pathway for a doctoral degree is offered jointly with the University of Nebraska at Lincoln (UNL). As the second largest HSI in the nation, UTR V is uniquely positioned to broaden the participation of Hispanics in the engineering workforce.
CONGRANT.OTHER_AGENCIES: The proposal focuses on increasing “effective STEM education and broadening participation” in underrepresented minority STEM students at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) to successfully face academic and professional challenges, recently exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The Freshman Year Innovator Experience proposes the development of self-transformation skills in freshman mechanical engineering students to successfully face academic and professional challenges exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic while working on two parallel projects of technical design innovation and academic career pathways.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Design, Construction, and Performance Monitoring of Stabilization of Expansive Soils and Cement
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Traditional methods to stabilize expansive soil and aggregate bases use either lime, cement, fly ash, emulsion, or combination. However, with high levels of sulfates in soils in many areas in Texas, the traditional stabilizers have faced some problems. Many major pavement failures have occurred due to lime or cement induced sulfate in soils. Studies including TxDOT research showed there are potential benefits of applying polypropylene fiber to stabilize expansive clays and cement treated bases to increase strength, reduce chemical stabilizer content, and increase flexibility/ductility. However, the construction procedures and related specifications are not fully developed. To evaluate this promising technology, this research project shall perform eight objectives: 1) Verify test methods and application rates to be tested in the field through laboratory testing; 2) Select construction and test sites, with preference given to the Paris District for test sites; 3) Plan test section construction; 4) Develop construction specifications; 5) Monitor construction of test sections and verify that specifications are followed; 6) Monitor construction test sections quantifying, at a minimum, profile, FWD, and crack counts for two years post construction; 7) Prepare workshop training modules on construction and test methods; and 8) Present training workshops.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Implementation of Advanced Geophysical Tools for Geotechnical Analysis
Sustainable long-term performance of geothermal energy foundations in hot climates
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Overview: More widespread use of geothermal energy has the potential to reduce energy usage and the nation’s CO2 footprint. A geothermal energy foundation can be used to heat and cool a building by using heat exchangers installed within the foundation to extract energy from the earth to heat the building in the winter, and to transfer excess heat into the earth to cool the building in the summer. Energy foundations cost up to 20% less to install compared to traditional ground source heat pump (GSHP) systems. By using “free” energy, geothermal foundations reduce heating and cooling costs by 50–70% compared with conventional heating and cooling systems. However, when heating and cooling loads are imbalanced, such as in warmer climates or in high-rise structures where internal heat generation requires greater cooling capacity, the heat transferred into the ground surpasses the heat extracted, and the temperature in the soil around the geothermal foundation will gradually increase from accumulated heat. Scientific understanding is limited regarding 1) how accumulated heat changes soil properties by driving moisture away, reducing soil thermal conductivity, and causing lower heat transfer rates, subsequently reducing the energy foundation’s efficiency; and 2) how complex volume changes in the energy foundation and surrounding soil (due to moisture loss and thermal expansion) can alter soil-foundation interactions, affect geotechnical functions of the foundation, and cause displacements of the foundation and ground surface. To maintain the sustainable performance of geothermal foundations, it is first necessary to understand these responses, and later, to identify and evaluate solutions for dissipating heat in imbalanced heating/cooling conditions. The hypothesis of this research project is that changes in soil properties caused by accumulated heat will cause energy foundations to stop functioning after several decades, and a greater rate of imbalanced heating and cooling will correspond with shorter time-to-failure intervals. The objective of this project is to develop a verified thermal-hydro-mechanical 3D model that can be used to assess the effects of long-term accumulated heat on energy foundations and the surrounding soil. The proposed simulation experiments will be conducted using a fully coupled model developed in COMSOL® Multiphysics.
Intellectual Merit: Findings from the proposed study will help the geothermal research community gain a better understanding of the effects of imbalanced heat on soil and geothermal energy foundations. Experimental data spanning 10 to 30 years are not available to study the long-term effects of accumulated heat in soil and energy foundations. Neither 3D modeling nor analytical solutions have addressed changes in soil properties caused by the foundation’s heat rejection, and therefore validated approaches are not available to address existing knowledge gaps. The planned activities will advance scientific knowledge by providing a more comprehensive understanding of the variables and conditions affecting energy foundation efficiency. These findings will also enable future investigations to explore changes in soil-foundation interactions (such as vertical and lateral load transfers), assess ground surface displacement, and evaluate solutions for reducing long-term heat accumulation in the surrounding ground. 
Broader Impacts: This proposal will yield two broad societal impacts. First, environmental and economic benefits will result from improved knowledge regarding the design, monitoring and maintenance of geothermal energy foundations. Effective design and use of these foundations reduces CO2 emissions, energy usage, and national reliance on non-renewable energy sources. Second, educational and outreach benefits from the integration of geothermal energy education in secondary and undergraduate settings will promote interest and engagement in STEM research.  The project will engage students in grades 8-11 in the Texas Pre-Freshman Engineering Program (TexPREP) with instruction provided by research assistants working on the proposed project.  Through the use of the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley’s Mobile Geothermal Educational Unit that was created for GSHP studies, the project also will increase public awareness of and engagement in STEM. All outreach activities will involve the PI’s interdisciplinary research team, which has thus far attracted two high school students and 28 civil, mechanical and electrical engineering undergraduate students (20% female and 94% Hispanic).

CONGRANT.TITLE: GOALI: A New Method and Device to Perform Particle Size Analysis for Geotechnical Engineering Investigations

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
High Efficiency Moisture Controlled Horizontal Energy Foundation
In 2016, about 40% or 39 quadrillion British thermal units (BTUs) of total U.S. energy was consumed by the residential and commercial sectors with heating and cooling systems making up 20% of this fraction [1]. An energy foundation harvests sustainable geothermal energy to heat and cool a building by integrating a ground heat exchanger into the building’s foundation. An energy foundation extracts heat from the ground in the winter to heat buildings and injects heat into the ground during the summer to cool buildings. Use of energy foundations to heat and cool buildings can reduce a large portion of U.S. energy consumption. The goal of this proposal is to develop an innovative high efficiency moisture-controlled horizontal energy foundation system for use in residential and commercial buildings. The energy foundation will save up to 20% of initial installation cost when compared with a traditional horizontal ground source heat pump system, and by using free energy, reduce heating and cooling costs by 50–70% when compared with a conventional heating and cooling system. To this end, the objective of this study is to optimize the system to provide significant cost saving. Three levels of testing to be conducted in parallel include:  full scale in-situ testing, model testing and specimen testing. The field and model testing is to understand system performance, and the specimen testing is to develop a new thermally enhanced nanofiber-cement grout. Three-dimensional computational modeling and probability analyses employing Monte-Carlo simulation will also be conducted to optimize system configuration and quantify the system’s reliability.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Earth Pressure Assessment and Optimization of Type-7 Barrier Geosynthetic Reinforced Soil Walls
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: With reference to the attached MSE/GRS worksheet B-504-S7, the extended height Type-7 barrier can be applied either for roadway grade separation at a median or as cut walls for a widened shoulder.  During design or construction if rock/very competent soil (OSHA construction and global stability requirements) were found, this worksheet would be applicable and result in direct benefits to the State. In additional to earth pressure, bearing capacity is also one of the design criteria when using a truncated 2’-0” base. Currently a tied rod with dead-man anchor at 5’-0” spacing is required for both rail impact and conservatism for unknowns including earth pressure. Current AASHTO MSE wall guidelines are limited with respect to design and earth pressure when utilizing Type-7 Barrier GRS walls. CDOT with this proposed research will assess the real earth pressure applied to the reinforced concrete barrier facing and establish a reasonable earth pressure for soil with tensile inclusions.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Energy Foundations' Heat Accumulation Impacts on Soil Properties, Structural Performance and Long Term System Efficiency
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Overview: A geothermal energy foundation harvests sustainable geothermal energy to heat and cool a building by using ground heat exchangers integrated into a building’s deep foundation that extracts energy from the earth to heat the building in the winter and injects excess heat into the earth to cool buildings in the summer. The energy foundation will save up to 20% of initial installation cost when compared with a traditional ground source heat pump (GSHP) system. By using this free energy, the energy foundation reduces heating and cooling costs by 50–70% compared with a conventional heating and cooling system. When the heat injected into the ground surpasses the heat extracted, or the cooling and heating load is imbalanced, the temperature in the soil around the energy foundation will gradually increase after each year of operation. There exists a lack of comprehensive understanding on i) how accumulated heat changes soil properties, drives moisture away, reduces soil thermal conductivity, and lowers the heat transfer rate resulting in a reduction of energy foundation efficiency, ii) how the complicated volume change in soil from moisture loss, thermal expanding and contracting, as well as how volume changes in the energy foundation can alter soil-foundation interaction and bearing capacity.
Intellectual Merit: Neither experimental data, 3D modeling, nor analytical solutions are available for long-term and large-scale analysis of a complete energy foundation to address the addressed lack of comprehensive understanding. The hypothesis of this research is that due to the changes in soil properties and heat transfer rate caused from the accumulated heat, the energy foundation will stop functioning after several decades.  The simulation experiment will be conducted using a coupled thermal-hydro-mechanical 3D model developed in COMSOL® Multiphysics. The validated model will be used to analyze the behaviors of soil and structures under a long-term imbalanced heat injection from an energy foundation with multiple energy piles, considering the effects of ground water movement. This helps achieve two research objectives 1) to understand the long-term behaviors of soil in terms of changes in temperature, moisture content, thermal conductivity and volume due to complex coupled thermal, hydraulic and mechanical interactions considering underground water movement and 2) to predict the long-term system performance of an energy foundation in terms of heat pump efficiency, foundation bearing capacity and stress, and settlement. The successful completion of this research will help the geothermal research community gain a comprehensive understanding of the effects of imbalanced heat on the soil and energy foundations.
Broader Impacts: The broader impacts of this proposal include two major areas: 1) The broader use of energy foundations has the potential to reduce energy cost and the nation’s CO2 footprint. 2) This project will integrate geothermal energy education with the Texas Pre-Freshman Engineering Program (TexPREP) and University of Texas Rio Grande Valley’s (UTRGV)’s Hispanic Engineering, Science, and Technology Week (HESTEC). The proposed educational plan will increase public awareness and engagement with STEM through the use of an available Mobile Geothermal Educational Unit created for GSHP studies, the HESTEC exhibit, and TexPREP field trips for students in Grades 8-11. All activities will involve the PI’s interdisciplinary research team, which has attracted 25 civil, mechanical and electrical engineering students, among them 20% are women and 89% are bilingual.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Synthesis of Load-Deflection Characteristics of Laterally Loaded Large Diameter Drilled Shafts
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: With the increasing of heavier and autonomous equipment, the drilled shaft diameters used for bridges are getting larger. Applicability of the traditional p-y models for large diameter drilled shafts requires additional investigation, since the models were developed decades ago based on experiments using smaller piles with diameters of one to two feet. The reliability of these early p-y models for predicting shaft deflection and moments for current project designs has caused concern.   The goal of this research is to provide TxDOT with a proposed modified p-y models that can produce reliable designs of large-diameter drilled shafts for bridge foundations with different soil conditions. The objective of this research is to provide TxDOT recommendations on the design of large diameter drilled shafts and  a synthesis of available reports, modeling, and data on the lateral loading of large diameter piles or drilled shafts (five feet and larger). The modified p-y curves will allow more accurate predictions of drilled shaft responses which takes into account the diameter influence.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Synthesis on Rapid Repair Methods for Embankment Slope Failures
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Embankment slope failures are one of the common stability issues on Texas highway structures. The main concern is that some repair attempts have shown a recurring failure of the repaired slope. To solve this problem, this research project has two set objectives:                 1) evaluation of the existing repair methods and 2) recommendation of appropriate implementation procedures for several rapid repair methods for slope failure. This research proposes the evaluation of the various methods used for rapid repair of embankment failures using the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP). The work plan starts by surveying the existing rapid repair methods, defining their attributes, and their relative importance. A survey will be designed to solicit the experts’ opinion regarding TxDOT preferences to determine the relative weights through pairwise comparisons. For the decision criteria of the cost and time, the method of slices and finite element methods with the most suitable parameter inputs shall be used to obtain the typical failure modes of recently damaged slopes in Texas. This study will document the procedures of the different repair methods used for the slope failure modes to ensure the satisfactory long-term performance of the repair.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Geothermal Energy for Safe and Healthy Communities:  An Environmentally Clean, Sustainable Alternative to Fossil Fuels
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This project is to support environmental education on geothermal energy usage in Rio Grande Valley, and  increase public awareness and knowledge about geothermal energy for safe, healthy, sustainable communities. Innovative usage of energy foundation that utilize geothermal energy for  heating and cooling  buildings will provide an environmentally clean, sustainable alternative to fossil fuels. The target audiences of high school and college students, 9-12 teachers, and communities such as retirement, veterans  all with large contingencies of Hispanic-Americans. The audience will be given verbal training supplemented with educational handouts about environmental issues , and will be provided with the skills that needed  to make informed environmental decisions and take responsible actions toward the environment. The general goal is to couple STEM-based principles with cutting-edge geothermal energy exchange engineering concepts used  to heat and cool buildings as a conceptual and practical foundation to increase environmental literacy, build environmental partnerships and create an ethic for safe, healthy, sustainable communities in the Rio Grand Valley. The audience will be site visit a geothermal site with a mobil educational unit that actually heated and cooled with geothermal energy. Results will be evaluated and analyzed during and subsequent to the project. This project involves two junior faculty and an experienced senior scientist with research and administrative experience in two federal agencies and the University of Missouri.

CONGRANT.TITLE: LEADERSHIP IN TRANSPORTATION INNOVATION  Multifunctional Carbon Nanofibers for Transportation Initiatives
Use of Geothermal Energy for Deicing Approach Pavement Slabs and Bridge Decks
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The objective of the proposed research task is to achieve significant and recurring cost savings for TxDOT through innovative recommendations on the design of a new system for snow and ice control for pavement slabs and bridge decks.  The research will investigate and provide recommendations on the use geothermal systems to store summer heat in the ground and reuse the energy in the winter to  keep the roadway pavement above freezing. The new system is based on a sustainable, renewable, and free energy from the earth. The system’s implementation not only will help with labor and maintenance expenses but also provide a service that is environmentally friendly.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: The Creation and Evaluation of an Engineering Student Leadership Academy
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: This article describes the creation and evaluation designed to support student success through their inclusion in a variety of professional and technical training programs. The opportunity to develop a leadership academy specifically for engineering students allowed faculty program coordinators to deliver content that was normally not available to students at this Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI). We implemented and evaluated the leadership academy using a mixed-methods approach involving multimedia interviews and two traditional survey data collection techniques. Traditional online surveys gave quick feedback to coordinators on what the students found valuable, with the biggest change in programming being the spreading out of the Engineering Student Leadership Academy (ESLA) from two days to four half-days over the course of a month. Assessing the change in students’ perception of leadership skills proved harder to measure in the short term. Using videoed interviews shortly after the delivery of the program had additional quality improvements, including the opportunity to showcase Hispanics, particularly Latinas, in leadership roles in the field of engineering. Reflections on improving the assessment and evaluation components are included in the article.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: NSF EEC: Establishing UTRGV's Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Hispanics are one of the fastest growing populations in the US, yet they are underrepresented in engineering. University X, a major Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) with a student population over 95% Hispanic, is well-positioned to address this disparity. University X established a Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich (CBPE-E3) to enhance Hispanic participation in engineering from early awareness through professional employment. The CBPE -E3 aims to increase enrollment, retention, and advancement rates of Hispanic students in higher education engineering, especially Latinas facing intersectional barriers of race and gender. The CBPE -E3 envisions becoming the leading national model for inclusion, professional preparation, and successful advancement of Hispanic engineers. Drawing on the community wealth asset framework, the CBPE -E3 is grounded in culturally relevant programming and pedagogy. It encompasses three objectives and related focus areas: 1) ENGAGE (K-12 Outreach): Provide early exposure to engineering content and role models for students, their families and communities, and teachers and counselors; 2) EDUCATE (Education & Training): Create an inclusive college experience that promotes students' success through curricular reform and trainings for faculty and students; and 3) ENRICH (Professional & Research Experiences): Provide the next generation of engineers with critical professional, leadership, and research development opportunities. The CBPE -E3 builds on University X's long-standing commitment to supporting Latinx students, as recognized with a 2021 Seal of Excelencia, and in broadening participation through successful NSF ADVANCE IT, INCLUDES, and ECR grants. It also leverages partnerships with 14 entities, including major universities, engineering professional societies, community colleges, K-12 systems, non-profits, and engineering employers and alumni. The CBPE -E3 expands University X's student educational opportunities through an R1 institution collaboration to create the Alliance for Student Participation in Research Experiences for Hispanics (ASPIRE Hispanics). It also introduces students to role models, professional networks, and ongoing personal and career development through professional society partners. Finally, the CBPE -E3 shares promising practices with institutions serving largely Hispanic populations so that they can replicate or adapt best practices at their home campuses through an "Equity in Engineering Education Summit." Infrastructure in phase I will be expanded for national scale-up in phase II. The authors will present the work in progress and preliminary results from a pilot implementation. This project is funded by NSF award 2217780.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Investigating shear behavior of cohesionless soils with the variation of particle sizes using Discrete Element Method
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: This research studies the effects of particle sizes and shapes on stress-strain behaviors for granular soils/ground rocks in triaxial test modelling by utilizing the discrete-element method (DEM) using PFC3D version 5.0. Spherical particles and non-spherical particles were considered, and larger particle sizes were varied while the minimum particle size was kept unchanged at 10mm. Results shows that shear strength varies with the change in particle size and complies with the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion, and that particle size has dominating effects on stress-strain behaviors of soils. Increasing the sizes of larger particles increases the stiffness and strength of granular specimens. When the maximum particle size increases from 20 mm to 50 mm, cohesion increases from 6 kPa to 11 kPa, and internal friction angle increases from 40.5° to 42.5°. Micro-mechanical investigation for the effects of the particle size on packing characteristics is also presented.

PRESENT.TITLE: Service limit state design procedure for drilled shafts in shales using t-z method
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: A new procedure is proposed for design of individual drilled shafts in shale at service limit states. The procedure utilizes t-z analyses and adopts the factored strength approach to account for variability and uncertainty in the design method and associated input parameters. The resistance factors used in the procedure were calibrated using a finite-element code to model load transfer in drilled shafts and Monte Carlo simulations. The variability and uncertainty considered for calibration of the resistance factors were derived from full-scale load tests performed on drilled shafts founded in shales in the central United States. The calibrated resistance factors generally range between 0.1 and 0.4, depending upon the uncertainty in the shale uniaxial compressive strength.  Such values are substantially less than those commonly used in current practice, but reasonably reflect the collective variability and uncertainty present for design of drilled shafts in shale. The primary appeal of the proposed procedure is that it eliminates the need to design for the service limit state on a case-by-case basis.
